data.name: Turner
data.detailed_description:
Turner is a 2D platformer puzzle game set in an insane asylum where you take the role of Turner, a man with a troubled past and an unstable state of mind. Complete over 500 levels by rotating the world around you. Solve a variety of puzzles, traverse through challenging levels, collect mysterious notes scattered throughout the asylum, and avoid dangerous obstacles, all while trying to solve the mystery of why you're there.

• Rotate the world at your will to make your way through the asylum.
• Learn new abilities, such as jumping off of walls or sliding under narrow passageways.
• 200+ original levels, 200+ challenge levels.
• 50 bonus levels, 50 challenge bonus levels.
• 500+ levels in total.
• Uncover the mystery that shrouds your past.
• "Comic book style" cutscenes.
• Use tools around you to solve puzzles while avoiding hazards such as security cameras, electric fences, and more.
• Original dark themed "sketch style” art.
• Original soundtrack.
• Full Controller support.
• Speedrun mode.

reviews.review:
Turner is a distinctive 2D puzzle-platformer that takes a familiar genre and gives it an unusual gravitational twist. Developed and published by Bean Boy Games, it places players inside a bleak asylum where the protagonist, Turner, must navigate hundreds of increasingly complicated rooms while gradually discovering clues about his situation. Rather than depending entirely on jumping accuracy, the game allows the environment itself to be rotated, changing the direction of gravity and transforming walls, floors, and ceilings into potential routes. This single mechanic forms the foundation of an experience that mixes spatial reasoning, traditional platforming, environmental hazards, and a modest psychological mystery.

Rotating the world is immediately intuitive but becomes increasingly demanding as the level designs grow more complicated. A platform that appears unreachable can suddenly become accessible when the room is turned, while a safe position can become dangerous once gravity shifts. Success therefore requires thinking about where Turner is standing now and where he will fall after the next rotation. The better puzzles encourage players to mentally reconstruct the entire room before committing to a move. Mistakes are part of the learning process, and discovering the correct sequence of rotations provides the satisfying realization expected from a good spatial puzzle.

The platforming becomes more involved as additional movement abilities enter the equation. Wall jumping and sliding expand Turner's mobility, allowing later stages to combine environmental manipulation with more conventional tests of timing and execution. Security cameras, electric fences, and other obstacles prevent the experience from becoming a simple exercise in rotating every room until an obvious path appears. Certain situations demand both a correct solution and accurate movement, giving the game a pleasant balance between puzzle solving and mechanical skill.

Content quantity is one of Turner's biggest strengths. The game contains more than 500 stages spread across its main levels, challenge levels, bonus stages, and bonus challenges. More than 200 standard levels establish the core journey, while a similarly substantial collection of challenge stages provides additional tests. There are also dozens of bonus levels and corresponding challenge variants. It is an impressive amount of material for a relatively modest indie production, particularly for players who enjoy completing puzzle games thoroughly. The downside is that such a large number of stages naturally leads to some repetition. The central mechanic remains entertaining, but playing for very long sessions can make certain environmental patterns feel overly familiar.

The asylum setting gives the adventure more personality than a completely abstract puzzle collection would have offered. Turner is trying to understand why he is confined there, and scattered notes reveal pieces of his history and surrounding circumstances. These discoveries add an exploratory incentive to the platforming while gradually developing the mystery. Comic-style cutscenes are used to communicate important narrative moments, fitting the game's stylized presentation without interrupting play for overly elaborate cinematic sequences. The storytelling is relatively straightforward, but it gives the extensive level progression a useful sense of context.

Visually, the game favors a dark, sketch-like presentation that complements its unsettling location. The artwork is deliberately rough rather than technically elaborate, producing an atmosphere that feels appropriate for the protagonist's strange journey. Its original soundtrack supports the same mood. Neither the graphics nor audio are particularly extravagant, yet they work together effectively enough to establish a recognizable identity. The relatively simple visual design also helps keep important platforms, obstacles, and hazards understandable during rooms where the entire environment is constantly changing orientation.

Replayability extends beyond completing the enormous level selection. A dedicated speedrun mode changes the nature of previously solved puzzles by encouraging players to complete them as efficiently as possible. Once the solution to a room has been learned, the challenge becomes executing rotations and movement without hesitation. Leaderboard support gives competitive players another reason to refine their routes, while achievements and trading cards provide additional progression for completion-focused Steam users. Full controller support is especially welcome for a platformer built around frequent movement and directional changes.

Turner is also extremely lightweight in terms of hardware requirements, so running the game should not be demanding on most modern computers. Steam Deck compatibility, however, is not officially categorized with a Verified or Playable rating on its Steam store listing. It should therefore be treated as Unverified for Steam Deck rather than assumed to have guaranteed handheld compatibility. The presence of full controller support and modest system requirements is encouraging, but these factors alone do not constitute official Deck certification, and individual compatibility may depend on Proton behavior and configuration.

The greatest achievement here is how extensively the game develops a concept that could easily have been little more than a short gimmick. Rotating levels fundamentally changes how ordinary platforming spaces are interpreted, and combining that ability with wall jumps, sliding, hazards, collectibles, challenge stages, and speedrunning provides meaningful variety. The unusually large stage count occasionally works against the pacing, and the presentation clearly reflects the game's small-scale indie origins, but neither issue eliminates the satisfaction of solving a cleverly constructed room.

Turner is ultimately a worthwhile puzzle-platformer for players who enjoy spatial challenges and unconventional gravity mechanics. Its enormous selection of stages provides considerable longevity, while the asylum mystery and scattered narrative material give some purpose to the journey beyond solving one puzzle after another. It may lack the refinement of larger productions, but its creative central mechanic, extensive content, optional challenges, and speedrunning possibilities make it considerably more ambitious than its understated appearance suggests.

Rating: 8/10
